evidence.excerpt: Instrumental resolution, spectral resolution, and pixel-scale reporting are internally inconsistent across the manuscript. The Abstract states observations at “∼113 pc arcsec−1 and 1.3 km s−1 spectral resolution,” while Sec. 2.1 gives CO(1–0) and CO(2–1) spectral resolutions of ∼2.6 and ∼1.27 km s−1, respectively. Sec. 2.1 also says the configuration provides ∼0.5″ resolution, but the final beams are 0.87″×0.80″ and 1.21″×1.04″. Appendix A.3 states CO(1–0) and CO(2–1) pixel sizes of 0.1″ and 0.14″, whereas Appendix A lists 0.12″ and 0.08″. This matters because the paper’s main claims depend on resolved offsets, linewidths, and matched CO comparisons.

evidence.excerpt: The CO(2–1)/CO(1–0) comparison with single-dish data is ambiguous and potentially inconsistent in definition. Sec. 3.4 defines R21 as an L′ ratio and obtains R21 = 0.34±0.22. Sec. 3.5 lists IRAM fluxes of 1.2 and 1.4 Jy km s−1; using the same L′ definition, these fluxes imply a ratio near 0.29 before any additional beam correction, yet Sec. 3.5 reports an IRAM R21 of 0.6 and an ALMA corrected value of 0.29. Without a clear distinction between brightness-temperature, flux-density, beam-matched, and L′ ratios, the statement that the ALMA ratio is “substantially lower than single-dish values” is hard to assess.

The paper explicitly defines “R21 = L′CO(2−1)/L′CO(1−0)” in Sec. 3.4, but later mixes this with a different single-dish ratio presentation: Sec. 3.5 gives IRAM fluxes of “1.2 and 1.4 Jy km s−1,” while Table 3 lists “Ratio R21 IRAM 0.6 beam corrected to 22″” and “Ratio Rcorr21 ALMA 0.29.” The manuscript does not clearly distinguish these as different conventions (L′ ratio vs beam-matched/brightness-temperature ratio), so the comparison to “single-dish values” is indeed ambiguous.

The reviewer correctly identifies a definitional inconsistency. Using the L′ ratio definition from Section 3.4, the single-dish fluxes of 1.2 and 1.4 Jy km s−1 yield an R21 of ~0.29, which exactly matches the ALMA corrected ratio. However, Table 3 reports an IRAM ratio of "0.6", making the claim in Section 3.5 that the ALMA ratio is "substantially lower than single-dish values" unsupported or mathematically flawed.
